video_script.label: High-retention hook
video_script.text: Applying for an internship but have no job experience? You can still make a strong student resume. In the next five minutes, we will build a clean one-page resume in Google Docs, turn a college project into evidence, and check the formatting before you export. By the end, you will know exactly what to write next, and what to leave out. Open a blank document and follow along.
video_script.visual: Show the completed one-page resume for two seconds, then switch to a blank Google Doc.

video_script.label: Module 1: Set up the document
video_script.text: First, open Google Docs and choose a blank document. Keep the page simple: one column, a readable font, and consistent headings. Avoid tables, icons, and multiple text boxes because they can make a resume harder to scan or edit. Put your name at the top, followed by your phone number, professional email, city, and a LinkedIn or portfolio link if it is ready. You do not need to include private details that are irrelevant to the role.
video_script.visual: Create a one-column layout and add a professional contact header.

video_script.label: Module 2: Write a short profile
video_script.text: Next, add a two-line profile that connects your current studies with the opportunity. Skip generic claims like hard-working student. Instead, mention your course, one relevant skill, and the kind of work you want to contribute to. For example: second-year computer science student who built a responsive event page using HTML and CSS, seeking a web-development internship to practise front-end skills. Use this only if it accurately describes you. Specific and truthful beats impressive-sounding but empty.
video_script.visual: Cross out a generic claim and reveal the specific sample profile.

video_script.label: Module 3: Turn a project into evidence
video_script.text: Here is the section that helps when you do not have a job history: projects. Name the project, add the tools you actually used, then write one or two bullets describing what you made and how it works. Use an action verb such as designed, analysed, coded, organized, or tested. Weak bullet: made a website. Stronger: built a three-page event website with HTML and CSS, including a registration form and mobile-friendly layout. Do not invent users, results, or numbers. If you have a measured result, include it; if not, describe the real output.
video_script.visual: Show before/after bullet; underline action + tool + output.

video_script.label: Module 4: Add education and skills
video_script.text: Add education with your degree, college, expected graduation year, and relevant coursework if it supports the role. Then list a small number of skills you can demonstrate. Group them if that helps: tools, programming languages, or communication skills. A skill list is not proof by itself, so connect important skills to a project or activity elsewhere on the page. Keep the most relevant items near the top and remove skills you cannot explain in an interview.
video_script.visual: Build Education and Skills headings; show only truthful, role-relevant skills.

video_script.label: Module 5: Final scan and export
video_script.text: Do one final scan: consistent dates, no spelling errors, readable spacing, and links that open. Save an editable copy, then download a PDF with a clear filename such as Ananya-Sharma-Resume.pdf. Your layout is a starting point; tailor the top skills and project bullets to each role.
video_script.visual: Tick the final checklist and export the PDF.

We make practical lessons for students: digital tools, beginner coding, and career skills you can use in class or in an internship application. The pinned comment includes a five-point resume checklist and official writing guidance. Before you go, comment with the project you want to include on your resume. We will use real student questions to plan the next tutorial.
